children.name: pinneapple_intent.compile
children.doc:
The Engineering Intent Compiler: a sentence in, a typed study contract out — or the questions it needs, or a
refusal that says what is missing.

The compiler is deterministic first. It reads every ``number unit`` pair with the parser ``pp.design`` already uses
(one parser, two consumers), gives each to the slot of the same dimension whose keywords are closest, and fills the
rest from the references the family declares. A value it cannot read and the family cannot default becomes a
question; nothing is ever made up.

A model can be plugged in behind :class:`IntentLLM` — anything with ``extract(text, schema) -> dict``. Its answer is
used only where it can be checked: the family must exist, and every value it proposes must come with a quote that
occurs in the sentence and contains the number. The deterministic reading always runs and wins on conflicts, so the
compiler works with no network and no model at all.

classes.name: IntentLLM
classes.doc: What the compiler needs from a model: a structured extraction, and nothing else.

methods.name: extract
methods.sig: (text: str, schema: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]

functions.name: normalise_units
functions.doc:
Rewrite the glued unit spellings of a request into the products the dimensional analyser reads.

``W/m2K`` becomes ``W/(m^2*K)``, ``W/mK`` becomes ``W/(m*K)``, ``Pa·s`` becomes ``Pa*s``; everything else is
left exactly as written, because rewriting a unit the user did not mean is worse than refusing to read it.

functions.name: schema
functions.doc: The JSON schema-shaped description of what a model may propose, for a prompt or an extraction call.

functions.name: compile_study
functions.sig: (text: str, *, answers: dict[str, Any] | None = None, family: str | StudyFamily | None = None, mode: str = MODE_SIMULATION, llm: IntentLLM | None = None, seed: int = 0) -> StudyContract | OutOfScope
functions.doc:
Compile a request into a :class:`~pinneapple_intent.contract.StudyContract`.

* ``answers`` fills the follow-up questions (``{slot: value}``, ``{slot: (value, unit)}`` or ``"70 degC"``).
* ``family`` forces a family instead of selecting one from the words.
* ``mode`` is ``simulation`` (analytic, numerical, convergence) or ``physics_ai`` (adds the surrogate rung).
  ``science`` is recognised and refused with what it would need, because the literature stage is not built.
* ``llm`` is optional; the deterministic compiler runs regardless and wins on conflicts.

children.summary: The Engineering Intent Compiler: a sentence in, a typed study contract out — or the questions it needs, or a refusal that says what is missing.

children.name: pinneapple_intent.contract
children.doc:
The intent contract: one typed, versioned description of a physics study, with the provenance of every value.

A :class:`StudyContract` is what the compiler produces from a sentence and what the runner consumes. It is the
intermediate representation the whole capability is built on, and it has three properties that matter:

* **It is self-contained.** Every value carries its SI quantity, its unit and where it came from (``stated``,
  ``answered``, ``defaulted`` with a source, ``missing``). A value nobody gave and no reference fixes is *not*
  invented: it becomes a question. The contract is therefore reconstructible without the agent that wrote it.
* **It is serialisable and addressable.** ``to_dict()`` is the whole document, ``id`` is its SHA-256, so a run, a
  report and a contract can be tied together by hash and replayed later.
* **It reuses the existing value vocabulary.** :class:`~pinneapple_design.intent.spec.Quantity`,
  :class:`~pinneapple_design.intent.spec.Slot`, :class:`~pinneapple_design.intent.spec.Question` and the
  provenance constants are the ones ``pp.design`` already uses, so there is one notion of "a number that knows where
  it came from" in the library and not two (see ``docs/strategy/STRATEGY_PHYSICS_AI.md``, decision D1).

The contract does not execute anything. :mod:`pinneapple_intent.execute` runs it; :mod:`pinneapple_intent.compile`
writes it.

classes.name: Provenance
classes.doc:
Where the contract came from: the sentence, the compiler that read it, the library that will run it.

``compiler`` is ``deterministic`` or ``llm+deterministic``; ``llm`` names the model when one was asked, and its
answer is kept here even when the deterministic parser overrode it, because "the LLM proposed 85 degC and the
text did not contain it" is part of the record.

methods.name: capture
methods.sig: (text: str, *, compiler: str = 'deterministic', llm: str = '', llm_note: str = '', seed: int = 0) -> Provenance

classes.name: Rung
classes.doc: One step of the fidelity ladder: what is solved, how, and what it needs to be installed.

classes.name: StudyContract
classes.doc:
A physics study, described well enough to be run again by someone who never saw the request.

``family`` names the registered :class:`~pinneapple_intent.families.Family` that supplies the equations, the
quantities it needs and the ladder. ``values`` are the filled slots. ``assumptions`` are the statements the
family makes that are *not* measured (a reported study lists them); ``limitations`` are what the study does not
cover, so a reader cannot take the result further than it goes.

methods.name: id
methods.doc: The SHA-256 of the document without its creation timestamp, so the same contract has the same id.

methods.name: answer
methods.doc:
A new contract with the follow-up answers filled in. ``name=(value, unit)``, ``name="70 degC"`` or
``name=value`` in the unit the question showed.

methods.name: table
methods.doc: One row per quantity, with the provenance a report has to show next to every number.

functions.name: canonical
functions.doc: The JSON text an id is computed from: sorted keys, no whitespace, stable floats.

children.summary: The intent contract: one typed, versioned description of a physics study, with the provenance of every value.

children.name: pinneapple_intent.execute
children.doc:
Running a contract: the fidelity ladder, the checks between its rungs, the decision, and the files that let
someone else replay it.

The runner is deliberately dumb. It walks the ladder the contract carries, asks the family for each rung, and turns
the family's checklines into a :class:`~pinneapple_analysis.trust.trust_report.TrustReport`, which already owns the
library's decision rule (a failed critical check is ``REJECT``, a failed non-critical one is ``REVIEW``, and a rung
that did not run lowers the coverage). Nothing here decides on its own whether a result is good.

What a run writes is the point of the whole capability: ``contract.json`` (what was asked and compiled),
``run.json`` (what ran, with its numbers and checks), ``report.md`` and any figures. :mod:`pinneapple_intent.replay`
rebuilds the run from those files alone, without an agent and without the sentence that started it.

classes.name: StudyRun
classes.doc: What one execution produced: the contract, the rungs that ran, the decision, and where the files are.

methods.name: qoi
methods.doc: The quantity of interest from the most reliable rung that ran: the solver, else the closed form.

functions.name: run_study
functions.sig: (contract: StudyContract, *, out_dir: str | None = None, rungs: tuple[str, ...] | None = None, progress: Callable[[str], None] | None = None) -> StudyRun
functions.doc:
Run the ladder of ``contract`` and return the :class:`StudyRun`.

A contract that still has open questions is refused: the runner never guesses the value it was not given.
``rungs`` overrides the ladder (for example to re-run only the surrogate); the decision then reports the rungs
that did not run as ``not_run``, lowering coverage rather than passing silently.

functions.name: study
functions.sig: (text: str, *, out_dir: str | None = None, answers: dict[str, Any] | None = None, family: str | StudyFamily | None = None, mode: str = 'simulation', llm: Any = None, seed: int = 0, rungs: tuple[str, ...] | None = None, progress: Callable[[str], None] | None = None)
functions.doc:
A sentence in, a run out: ``compile_study`` and ``run_study`` in one call.

Returns the :class:`StudyRun` when the request compiled, or the contract carrying its questions (status
``needs_clarification``) or the refusal, so a caller always gets an object that says what happened and why.

children.summary: Running a contract: the fidelity ladder, the checks between its rungs, the decision, and the files that let someone else replay it.

children.name: pinneapple_intent.families
pinneapple_intent.families.beam_cantilever
children.doc:
Bending of a cantilever beam under a tip load.

The closed form is Euler-Bernoulli beam theory, which is exact for a slender beam and neglects shear. The solver is
the library's immersed finite-cell elasticity on the two-dimensional section, which is **plane strain** — so the
modulus the closed form must use is ``E / (1 - nu^2)``, not ``E``. Getting that convention wrong is the classic way
this comparison is made to look better or worse than it is; the family states it, uses it, and puts it in the report.

References: Euler (1744) and Bernoulli for the elastic curve; Timoshenko, *Strength of Materials*, part I, ch. 5, for
the cantilever with an end load and for the shear correction the closed form omits; Boresi & Chong, *Elasticity*, for
plain strain replacing ``E`` with ``E / (1 - nu^2)``.

methods.name: length_scale
methods.doc: The section depth: the bending gradient is across it, so the grid has to resolve it, not the span.

methods.name: evaluate
methods.sig: (rung: str, contract: StudyContract, *, workdir: str | None = None, options: dict[str, Any] | None = None) -> Measurement

functions.name: closed_form
functions.sig: (length: float, height: float, depth: float, youngs_modulus: float, poisson: float, load: float) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Tip deflection of a cantilever on the plane-strain convention the two-dimensional solver uses.

``delta = P L^3 / (3 E' I)`` with ``E' = E / (1 - nu^2)`` and ``I = h^3 / 12`` for one metre of depth; ``P`` is
the tip load per metre of depth, which is how the two-dimensional model feels it.

children.summary: Bending of a cantilever beam under a tip load.

children.name: pinneapple_intent.families.heat_wall
children.doc:
Heat conduction through a wall, with convection on the cold side.

The study answers one question — how hot does the far face run — and answers it three times: by the series
resistance of one-dimensional steady conduction (exact when the wall is thin against its width and the edges are
insulated, which is the assumption the family states), by the immersed finite-cell solver on the real two-dimensional
wall, and by the same solver on a second grid so the discretisation error is visible rather than assumed.

Reference: Incropera & DeWitt, *Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer*, the one-dimensional plane wall with a
convection boundary (the series-resistance result ``q'' = (T_h - T_inf) / (L/k + 1/h)``).

methods.name: length_scale
methods.doc: The wall's own thickness: a grid coarser than that cannot show the gradient through it.

methods.name: evaluate
methods.sig: (rung: str, contract: StudyContract, *, workdir: str | None = None, options: dict[str, Any] | None = None) -> Measurement

functions.name: closed_form
functions.sig: (thickness: float, conductivity: float, hot_side: float, ambient: float, h_conv: float) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
One-dimensional steady conduction through the wall with convection on the far face.

``q'' = (T_hot - T_ambient) / (L/k + 1/h)`` and the far face sits at ``T_ambient + q''/h``. The wall's own
resistance and the film resistance add in series, which is the whole physics of this study.

children.summary: Heat conduction through a wall, with convection on the cold side.

children.name: pinneapple_intent.families.laminar_pipe
children.doc:
Pressure drop of a laminar flow along a circular pipe.

Three answers to the same question. The closed form is Hagen-Poiseuille, which is exact when the flow is steady,
fully developed and laminar. The numerical rung solves the radial momentum balance of that flow by finite
differences on the real radius (wall no-slip, symmetry on the axis) and integrates the profile to the flow rate, so
it never uses the formula it is checked against. The convergence rung refines the radial grid. ``physics_ai`` mode
adds a surrogate of the pressure drop over the pipe length.

References: Hagen (1839) and Poiseuille (1840) for the law; White, *Viscous Fluid Flow*, ch. 3, for the derivation
and the friction factor ``f = 64/Re``.

methods.name: evaluate
methods.sig: (rung: str, contract: StudyContract, *, workdir: str | None = None, options: dict[str, Any] | None = None) -> Measurement

functions.name: hagen_poiseuille
functions.sig: (diameter: float, length: float, flow_rate: float, viscosity: float, density: float) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc: ``dp = 8 mu L Q / (pi R^4)`` with the Reynolds number and the mean velocity that say whether it applies.

functions.name: radial_profile
functions.sig: (diameter: float, length: float, flow_rate: float, viscosity: float, n: int) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Solve ``(1/r) d/dr (r du/dr) = (1/mu) dp/dx`` by finite differences and return the pressure drop that the
integrated profile implies for the requested flow rate.

The equation is linear in ``dp/dx``, so it is solved once for a unit gradient and the answer is scaled: the
integrated flow rate per unit gradient gives the gradient that carries ``flow_rate``. The discretisation is the
conservative one — fluxes at the cell faces, ``r`` weighted — so the symmetry condition on the axis is the flux
across ``r = 0`` being zero rather than an assumption about the first node.

children.summary: Pressure drop of a laminar flow along a circular pipe.

children.doc:
The built-in study families, and the registry they plug into.

    from pinneapple_intent.families import builtin
    [f.name for f in builtin()]     # ['beam_cantilever', 'heat_wall', 'laminar_pipe']

A new domain adds a module here that subclasses
:class:`~pinneapple_intent.family.StudyFamily`, implements ``evaluate``, and is returned by :func:`builtin`. The
guide (``docs/guides/intent_to_study.md``) walks through it.

functions.name: builtin
functions.doc: The families this release ships, in the order a request is matched against them.

children.summary: The built-in study families, and the registry they plug into.

children.name: pinneapple_intent.family
children.doc:
What a study family is: the physics knowledge that turns a filled contract into runs, checks and prose.

A family is the unit a new domain plugs in with. It declares

* the words that select it (``keywords``) and the values it can read from a sentence (``slots``) — the same
  :class:`~pinneapple_design.intent.spec.Slot` ``pp.design`` uses, so one sentence reads the same way in both;
* the governing equations, the assumptions behind them, what the study does not cover, and the references the
  analytic rung is compared against — all of them printed in the report, because a result without its assumptions is
  not a result;
* the **fidelity ladder**: an analytic rung (closed form or a cited reference), a numerical rung (a real solver in the
  library), a convergence rung (the same solver refined, with the measured change) and, for ``physics_ai`` mode, a
  surrogate rung trained on the solver and scored on held-out designs;
* the quantity of interest (``qoi``) each rung reports, so the ladder can be compared rung against rung.

The contract the family reads is written by :mod:`pinneapple_intent.compile`; the ladder is driven by
:mod:`pinneapple_intent.execute`. A family never invents a value: everything it computes comes from a closed form, a
solver call, or a number the contract carries with its provenance.

classes.name: Measurement
classes.doc:
What one rung produced: the quantity of interest, the checklines, and the evidence it left in ``workdir``.

``checks`` follow the shape the rest of the library uses (``name``, ``passed``, ``value``, ``limit``,
``detail``), so a study's checks can be read next to a trust card's without translation.

classes.name: StudyFamily
classes.doc: Base class. Subclasses set the class attributes and implement :meth:`evaluate`.

methods.name: rungs
methods.doc: The ladder this family offers, filtered by mode: ``surrogate`` only when the study asks for Physics AI.

methods.name: length_scale
methods.doc: The smallest length the grid has to resolve; a family overrides it with the case's own dimension.

methods.name: spacing
methods.doc:
The grid spacing of a rung, derived from the case rather than fixed: a grid that does not resolve the
section is the usual reason a solver "disagrees" with a closed form it should reproduce.

methods.name: check_scope
methods.doc: Parts of the request this family cannot address (empty = in scope).

methods.name: default_objectives
methods.doc: A study has no objective to optimise; the attribute exists so the shared parser can read this family.

methods.name: evaluate
methods.sig: (rung: str, contract: StudyContract, *, workdir: str | None = None, options: dict[str, Any] | None = None) -> Measurement

methods.name: compare
methods.doc: The cross-rung checks: does the solver reproduce the closed form, and does it survive refinement?

functions.name: check
functions.sig: (name: str, passed: bool, *, value: Any = None, limit: Any = None, detail: str = '') -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: One checkline. ``limit`` is the number it was judged against, so a reader can re-judge it.

functions.name: select_family
functions.doc:
The family whose keywords are closest in ``text``, and the ranked alternatives (name, score).

A request whose best score is below :data:`MIN_SCORE` selects nothing: the compiler then refuses with the words
it could not place, instead of running the nearest study on it.

children.summary: What a study family is: the physics knowledge that turns a filled contract into runs, checks and prose.

children.name: pinneapple_intent.replay
children.doc:
Rebuild a study from the files it left behind, with no agent and no sentence.

The point of the contract is this module. If a run cannot be reproduced from ``contract.json`` alone, the contract is
missing something; if it reproduces to different numbers, either the library changed or the run was not
deterministic, and both are worth knowing before anyone acts on the result.

    python -m pinneapple_intent replay runs/heat_wall-1a03dab1

A replay compares the quantity of interest and every rung's outputs with the recorded values, and reports the
differences it found instead of a single "ok".

classes.name: ReplayResult
classes.doc: What a replay found: the new run, the recorded one, and every number that did not come back the same.

functions.name: replay
functions.sig: (path: str, *, out_dir: str | None = None, strict: bool = False) -> ReplayResult
functions.doc:
Re-run the study recorded in ``path`` (a run directory or its ``run.json``) and compare it with the record.

``strict`` raises when the replay does not match; by default the differences are returned so a caller can report
them with the numbers attached, which is more useful than an exception.

children.summary: Rebuild a study from the files it left behind, with no agent and no sentence.

doc:
PINNeAPPle Intelligence: a sentence in, a verified and replayable physics study out.

    import pinneapple as pp
    run = pp.study("a 12 mm steel wall, k = 200 W/mK, 300 degC inside, air at 25 degC outside, h = 12 W/m2K")
    print(run.summary())            # cold_face_temperature = 572.953 K (APPROVED); 6/6 checks passed
    run.files["report"]             # the Markdown report; contract.json and run.json sit next to it

    pp.study("a heat sink for a 40 W chip")     # -> the contract, status needs_clarification, with its questions

Three modes over one machinery:

* ``simulation`` — analytic, numerical and refinement rungs: a problem described in words becomes a solved and
  checked case.
* ``physics_ai`` — the same ladder plus a surrogate trained on the solver and scored on designs held out of its fit.
* ``science`` — recognised and refused with what it would need: the literature stage is not built yet.

The stages, each a typed object:

===========================  ===============================================================================
:mod:`.contract`             ``StudyContract``: the typed, versioned description of the study, with the provenance
                             of every value (``stated`` / ``answered`` / ``defaulted`` with its source /
                             ``missing``). Serialisable, addressable by SHA-256, reconstructible without an agent.
:mod:`.family`               ``StudyFamily``: the physics knowledge — slots, equations, assumptions, limitations,
                             references and the fidelity ladder. ``families()`` lists the installed ones.
:mod:`.compile`              ``compile_study(text)``: the Engineering Intent Compiler. Deterministic first, an LLM
                             optional behind ``IntentLLM``, and a refusal with what is missing when nothing fits.
:mod:`.execute`              ``run_study(contract)`` / ``study(text)``: walks the ladder, turns the checklines into a
                             ``TrustReport`` decision, writes ``contract.json``, ``run.json`` and ``report.md``.
:mod:`.replay`               ``replay(run_dir)``: rebuilds the run from its files and reports every number that did
                             not come back the same.

The rule the whole capability is built on: the model plans and proposes, the deterministic compiler and the solvers
check and execute. No value is invented, no result is reported without the checks that make it a result, and every
run can be rebuilt from its contract alone.
summary: PINNeAPPle Intelligence: a sentence in, a verified and replayable physics study out.
